title: Choose a chunking strategy and size that keep conditions with their rules, preserve source metadata, and balance matching precision against missing context

questions.prompt:
A RAG system indexes an internal policy corpus. Each chunk is embedded as one vector, and the top-matching chunks are passed to the model. The team shrinks chunks from about 800 tokens to about 150 tokens and changes nothing else.

Afterwards, the chunk containing the relevant rule ranks first more often. However, answers more often leave out exceptions that appear just after a rule in the source, such as "Keep logs for 90 days. Exception: security investigations require 365 days."

Explain why the smaller chunks cause **both** effects.

rubric.point: Better ranking: a small chunk covers roughly one idea, so its single vector represents that idea sharply and matches the query more precisely. A large chunk mixes several ideas, which dilutes its vector.
Missing exceptions: the smaller boundary can put the exception in a different chunk from its rule. Only the rule's chunk is retrieved, so the model never sees the condition that changes it.

questions.model:
Small chunks rank better because each 150-token chunk holds roughly one idea, so its one embedding represents that idea sharply. An 800-token chunk blends several ideas into one diluted vector.

The same small boundary can split the rule from the exception that follows it. The exception goes into a neighbouring chunk that doesn't match the query as well, so only the rule is retrieved and the answer leaves out the condition.

questions.prompt: During ingestion, a structure-aware splitter attaches metadata from the document's structure to every chunk it creates: the document ID and the heading path, such as `Data Retention > Exceptions`. Why is storing this metadata on each chunk useful?
options: It lets the splitter keep a rule and its exception together, because chunks that share a heading path are merged into one chunk before embedding.
It replaces chunk overlap, because the heading path tells the model which text sat on either side of each chunk boundary.
It lets retrieval filter results by section, and it lets a cited chunk be traced to its exact place in the source document.
It limits chunk size, because the splitter splits a chunk again whenever its heading path is longer than the embedding model's input limit.

rubric.point: Chooses the option saying that inherited metadata enables section-level filtering and traceable citations.

questions.model: **It lets retrieval filter results by section, and it lets a cited chunk be traced to its exact place in the source document.** The chunk's text alone may not show which document or section it came from. Adding this metadata during ingestion is cheaper than reconstructing it later.

c1.text: The search now more precise, because vectore have more focused meaning in it, but chunks doesnt contain the related info about exception because it cutted out by smaller chunks, which is not retrieved. The fix could be recursive chunking, increasing chunk size with and overlap or if possible, store exceptions or additional info as metadata which can be also retrieved

annotations.quote: The search now more precise, because vectore have more focused meaning in it
annotations.note: You link the better ranking to chunks having a more focused meaning. That matches the idea that a small chunk's single vector represents one idea sharply.

annotations.quote: chunks doesnt contain the related info about exception because it cutted out by smaller chunks, which is not retrieved
annotations.note: You explain that the smaller chunks cut the exception off from its rule, and that the exception's chunk is then not retrieved. That is the mechanism for the missing exceptions.

annotations.quote: The fix could be recursive chunking, increasing chunk size with and overlap
annotations.note: Overlap, larger chunks and structure-aware splitting are real mitigations for splitting a rule from its exception. The question didn't ask for fixes, so they earned no marks.

c1.feedback: Both effects are explained: focused vectors improve ranking, and the split separates the exception from its rule so it is never retrieved.
